1	---
2	title: Expand-and-contract migrations
3	description: Learn how to perform data migrations using the expand and contract pattern with Prisma ORM
4	image: /img/guides/data-migration-cover.png
5	url: /guides/database/data-migration
6	metaTitle: How to migrate data with Prisma ORM using the expand and contract pattern
7	metaDescription: Learn how to perform data migrations using the expand and contract pattern with Prisma ORM
8	---
9	
10	## Introduction
11	
12	When making changes to your database schema in production, it's crucial to ensure data consistency and avoid downtime. This guide shows you how to use the expand and contract pattern to safely migrate data between columns. We'll walk through a practical example of replacing a boolean field with an enum field while preserving existing data.
13	
14	## Prerequisites
15	
16	Before starting this guide, make sure you have:
17	
18	- Node.js installed (version 20 or higher)
19	- A Prisma ORM project with an existing schema
20	- A supported database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, etc.)
21	- Access to both development and production databases
22	- Basic understanding of Git branching
23	- Basic familiarity with TypeScript
24	
25	## 1. Set up your environment
26	
27	### 1.1. Review initial schema
28	
29	Start with a basic schema containing a Post model:
30	
31	```prisma
32	generator client {
33	  provider = "prisma-client"
34	  output   = "./generated/prisma"
35	}
36	
37	datasource db {
38	  provider = "postgresql"
39	}
40	
41	model Post {
42	  id        Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
43	  title     String
44	  content   String?
45	  published Boolean @default(false)
46	}
47	```
48	
49	### 1.2. Configure Prisma
50	
51	Create a `prisma.config.ts` file in the root of your project with the following content:
52	
53	```typescript title="prisma.config.ts"
54	import "dotenv/config";
55	import { defineConfig, env } from "prisma/config";
56	
57	export default defineConfig({
58	  schema: "prisma/schema.prisma",
59	  migrations: {
60	    path: "prisma/migrations",
61	  },
62	  datasource: {
63	    url: env("DATABASE_URL"),
64	  },
65	});
66	```
67	
68	:::note
69	
70	You'll need to install the required packages. If you haven't already, install them using your package manager:
71	
72	```npm
73	npm install prisma@7.10.0 @types/pg --save-dev
74	```
75	
76	```npm
77	npm install @prisma/client@7.10.0 @prisma/adapter-pg pg dotenv
78	```
79	
80	If you are using a different database provider (MySQL, SQL Server, SQLite), install the corresponding driver adapter package instead of `@prisma/adapter-pg`. For more information, see [Database drivers](/orm/v7/core-concepts/supported-databases/database-drivers).
81	
82	:::
83	
84	### 1.3. Create a development branch
85	
86	Create a new branch for your changes:
87	
88	```bash
89	git checkout -b create-status-field
90	```
91	
92	## 2. Expand the schema
93	
94	### 2.1. Add new column
95	
96	Update your schema to add the new Status enum and field:
97	
98	```prisma
99	model Post {
100	  id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
101	  title     String
102	  content   String?
103	  published Boolean? @default(false)
104	  status    Status   @default(Unknown)
105	}
106	
107	enum Status {
108	  Unknown
109	  Draft
110	  InProgress
111	  InReview
112	  Published
113	}
114	```
115	
116	### 2.2. Create migration
117	
118	Generate the migration:
119	
120	```npm
121	npx prisma migrate dev --name add-status-column
122	```
123	
124	Then generate Prisma Client:
125	
126	```npm
127	npx prisma generate
128	```
129	
130	## 3. Migrate the data
131	
132	### 3.1. Create migration script
133	
134	Create a new TypeScript file for the data migration:
135	
136	```typescript
137	import { PrismaClient } from "../generated/prisma/client";
138	import { PrismaPg } from "@prisma/adapter-pg";
139	import "dotenv/config";
140	
141	const adapter = new PrismaPg({
142	  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
143	});
144	
145	const prisma = new PrismaClient({
146	  adapter,
147	});
148	
149	async function main() {
150	  await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
151	    const posts = await tx.post.findMany();
152	    for (const post of posts) {
153	      await tx.post.update({
154	        where: { id: post.id },
155	        data: {
156	          status: post.published ? "Published" : "Unknown",
157	        },
158	      });
159	    }
160	  });
161	}
162	
163	main()
164	  .catch(async (e) => {
165	    console.error(e);
166	    process.exit(1);
167	  })
168	  .finally(async () => await prisma.$disconnect());
169	```
170	
171	### 3.2. Set up migration script
172	
173	Add the migration script to your package.json:
174	
175	```json
176	{
177	  "scripts": {
178	    "data-migration:add-status-column": "tsx ./prisma/migrations/<migration-timestamp>/data-migration.ts"
179	  }
180	}
181	```
182	
183	### 3.3. Execute migration
184	
185	1. Update your DATABASE_URL to point to the production database
186	2. Run the migration script:
187	
188	```npm
189	npm run data-migration:add-status-column
190	```
191	
192	## 4. Contract the schema
193	
194	### 4.1. Create cleanup branch
195	
196	Create a new branch for removing the old column:
197	
198	```bash
199	git checkout -b drop-published-column
200	```
201	
202	### 4.2. Remove old column
203	
204	Update your schema to remove the published field:
205	
206	```prisma
207	model Post {
208	  id      Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
209	  title   String
210	  content String?
211	  status  Status   @default(Unknown)
212	}
213	
214	enum Status {
215	  Draft
216	  InProgress
217	  InReview
218	  Published
219	}
220	```
221	
222	### 4.3. Generate cleanup migration
223	
224	Create and run the final migration:
225	
226	```npm
227	npx prisma migrate dev --name drop-published-column
228	```
229	
230	Then generate Prisma Client:
231	
232	```npm
233	npx prisma generate
234	```
235	
236	## 5. Deploy to production
237	
238	### 5.1. Set up deployment
239	
240	Add the following command to your CI/CD pipeline:
241	
242	```npm
243	npx prisma migrate deploy
244	```
245	
246	### 5.2. Monitor deployment
247	
248	Watch for any errors in your logs and monitor your application's behavior after deployment.
249	
250	## Troubleshooting
251	
252	### Common issues and solutions
253	
254	1. **Migration fails due to missing default**
255	   - Ensure you've added a proper default value
256	   - Check that all existing records can be migrated
257	
258	2. **Data loss prevention**
259	   - Always backup your database before running migrations
260	   - Test migrations on a copy of production data first
261	
262	3. **Transaction rollback**
263	   - If the data migration fails, the transaction will automatically rollback
264	   - Fix any errors and retry the migration
265	
266	## Next steps
267	
268	Now that you've completed your first expand and contract migration, you can:
269	
270	- Learn more about [Prisma Migrate](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate)
271	- Explore [schema prototyping](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/prototyping-your-schema)
272	- Understand [customizing migrations](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/customizing-migrations)
273	
274	For more information:
275	
276	- [Expand and Contract Pattern Documentation](https://www.prisma.io/dataguide/types/relational/expand-and-contract-pattern)
277	- [Prisma Migrate Workflows](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/development-and-production)
278

---
title: Expand-and-contract migrations
description: Learn how to perform data migrations using the expand and contract pattern with Prisma ORM
image: /img/guides/data-migration-cover.png
url: /guides/database/data-migration
metaTitle: How to migrate data with Prisma ORM using the expand and contract pattern
metaDescription: Learn how to perform data migrations using the expand and contract pattern with Prisma ORM
---

## Introduction

When making changes to your database schema in production, it's crucial to ensure data consistency and avoid downtime. This guide shows you how to use the expand and contract pattern to safely migrate data between columns. We'll walk through a practical example of replacing a boolean field with an enum field while preserving existing data.

## Prerequisites

Before starting this guide, make sure you have:

- Node.js installed (version 20 or higher)
- A Prisma ORM project with an existing schema
- A supported database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, etc.)
- Access to both development and production databases
- Basic understanding of Git branching
- Basic familiarity with TypeScript

## 1. Set up your environment

### 1.1. Review initial schema

Start with a basic schema containing a Post model:

```prisma
generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client"
  output   = "./generated/prisma"
}

datasource db {
  provider = "postgresql"
}

model Post {
  id        Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
  title     String
  content   String?
  published Boolean @default(false)
}
```

### 1.2. Configure Prisma

Create a `prisma.config.ts` file in the root of your project with the following content:

```typescript title="prisma.config.ts"
import "dotenv/config";
import { defineConfig, env } from "prisma/config";

export default defineConfig({
  schema: "prisma/schema.prisma",
  migrations: {
    path: "prisma/migrations",
  },
  datasource: {
    url: env("DATABASE_URL"),
  },
});
```

:::note

You'll need to install the required packages. If you haven't already, install them using your package manager:

```npm
npm install prisma@7.10.0 @types/pg --save-dev
```

```npm
npm install @prisma/client@7.10.0 @prisma/adapter-pg pg dotenv
```

If you are using a different database provider (MySQL, SQL Server, SQLite), install the corresponding driver adapter package instead of `@prisma/adapter-pg`. For more information, see [Database drivers](/orm/v7/core-concepts/supported-databases/database-drivers).

:::

### 1.3. Create a development branch

Create a new branch for your changes:

```bash
git checkout -b create-status-field
```

## 2. Expand the schema

### 2.1. Add new column

Update your schema to add the new Status enum and field:

```prisma
model Post {
  id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  title     String
  content   String?
  published Boolean? @default(false)
  status    Status   @default(Unknown)
}

enum Status {
  Unknown
  Draft
  InProgress
  InReview
  Published
}
```

### 2.2. Create migration

Generate the migration:

```npm
npx prisma migrate dev --name add-status-column
```

Then generate Prisma Client:

```npm
npx prisma generate
```

## 3. Migrate the data

### 3.1. Create migration script

Create a new TypeScript file for the data migration:

```typescript

import { PrismaPg } from "@prisma/adapter-pg";
import "dotenv/config";

  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
});

const prisma = new PrismaClient({
  adapter,
});

async function main() {
  await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
    const posts = await tx.post.findMany();
    for (const post of posts) {
      await tx.post.update({
        where: { id: post.id },
        data: {
          status: post.published ? "Published" : "Unknown",
        },
      });
    }
  });
}

main()
  .catch(async (e) => {
    console.error(e);
    process.exit(1);
  })
  .finally(async () => await prisma.$disconnect());
```

### 3.2. Set up migration script

Add the migration script to your package.json:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "data-migration:add-status-column": "tsx ./prisma/migrations/<migration-timestamp>/data-migration.ts"
  }
}
```

### 3.3. Execute migration

1. Update your DATABASE_URL to point to the production database
2. Run the migration script:

```npm
npm run data-migration:add-status-column
```

## 4. Contract the schema

### 4.1. Create cleanup branch

Create a new branch for removing the old column:

```bash
git checkout -b drop-published-column
```

### 4.2. Remove old column

Update your schema to remove the published field:

```prisma
model Post {
  id      Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  title   String
  content String?
  status  Status   @default(Unknown)
}

enum Status {
  Draft
  InProgress
  InReview
  Published
}
```

### 4.3. Generate cleanup migration

Create and run the final migration:

```npm
npx prisma migrate dev --name drop-published-column
```

Then generate Prisma Client:

```npm
npx prisma generate
```

## 5. Deploy to production

### 5.1. Set up deployment

Add the following command to your CI/CD pipeline:

```npm
npx prisma migrate deploy
```

### 5.2. Monitor deployment

Watch for any errors in your logs and monitor your application's behavior after deployment.

## Troubleshooting

### Common issues and solutions

1. **Migration fails due to missing default**
   - Ensure you've added a proper default value
   - Check that all existing records can be migrated

2. **Data loss prevention**
   - Always backup your database before running migrations
   - Test migrations on a copy of production data first

3. **Transaction rollback**
   - If the data migration fails, the transaction will automatically rollback
   - Fix any errors and retry the migration

- Learn more about [Prisma Migrate](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate)
- Explore [schema prototyping](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/prototyping-your-schema)
- Understand [customizing migrations](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/customizing-migrations)

For more information:

- [Expand and Contract Pattern Documentation](https://www.prisma.io/dataguide/types/relational/expand-and-contract-pattern)
- [Prisma Migrate Workflows](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/development-and-production)

For example, you might add an index directly to a production database to resolve an issue with a slow-running query. 10 11 Patching the production database directly results in **schema drift**: your database schema has 'drifted away' from the source of truth, and is out of sync with your migration history. You can use the `prisma migrate resolve` command to reconcile your migration history _without_ having to remove and re-apply the hotfix with `prisma migrate deploy`. 12 13 :::warning 14 This guide **does not apply for MongoDB**.
15 Instead of `migrate dev`, [`db push`](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/prototyping-your-schema) is used for [MongoDB](/orm/v7/core-concepts/supported-databases/mongodb). 16 ::: 17 18 ## Reconciling your migration history with a patch or hotfix 19 20 The following scenario assumes that you made a manual change in production and want to propagate that change to your migration history and other databases. 21 22 To reconcile your migration history and database schema in production: 23 24 - Replicate the change you made in production in the schema - for example, add an `@@index` to a particular model. 25 - Generate a new migration and take note of the full migration name, including a timestamp, which is written to the CLI:(`20210316150542_retroactively_add_index`): 26 27 ```npm 28 npx prisma migrate dev --name retroactively-add-index 29 ``` 30 31 ```bash no-copy 32 migrations/ 33 └─ 20210316150542_retroactively_add_index/ 34 └─ migration.sql 35 36 Your database is now in sync with your schema. 37 38 ✔ Generated Prisma Client (2.19.0-dev.29) to .\node_modules\@prisma\client in 190ms 39 ``` 40 41 - Push the migration to production **without running `migrate deploy`**. Instead, mark the migration created in the previous step as 'already applied' so that Prisma Migrate does not attempt to apply your hotfix a second time: 42 43 ```npm 44 npx prisma migrate resolve --applied "20201127134938-retroactively-add-index" 45 ``` 46 47 This command adds the migration to the migration history table without running the actual SQL. 48 49 - Repeat the previous step for other databases that were patched - for example, if you applied the patch to a staging database. 50 - Propagate the migration to other databases that were not patched - for example, by committing the migration to source control and allowing your CI/CD pipeline to apply it to all databases. The migration will not be applied to databases where it has been marked as already applied by the `prisma migrate resolve` command. 51 52 ## Failed migration 53 54 A migration might fail if: 55 56 - You [modify a migration before running it](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/workflows/customizing-migrations) and introduce a syntax error 57 - You add a mandatory (`NOT NULL`) column to a table that already has data 58 - The migration process stopped unexpectedly 59 - The database shut down in the middle of the migration process 60 61 Each migration in the `_prisma_migrations` table has a `logs` column that stores the error. 62 63 There are two ways to deal with failed migrations in a production environment: 64 65 - Roll back, optionally fix issues, and re-deploy 66 - Manually complete the migration steps and resolve the migration 67 68 ### Option 1: Mark the migration as rolled back and re-deploy 69 70 The following example demonstrates how to roll back a migration, optionally make changes to fix the issue, and re-deploy: 71 72 - Mark the migration as rolled back - this updates the migration record in the `_prisma_migrations` table to register it as rolled back, allowing it to be applied again: 73 74 ```npm 75 npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back "20201127134938_added_bio_index" 76 ``` 77 78 - If the migration was partially run, you can either: 79 - Modify the migration to check if a step was already completed (for example: `CREATE TABLE ... IF NOT EXISTS`) _OR_ 80 - Manually revert the steps that were completed (for example, delete created tables) 81 82 If you modify the migration, make sure you copy it back to source control to ensure that state of your production database is reflected exactly in development. 83 84 - Fix the root cause of the failed migration, if relevant - for example, if the migration failed due to an issue with the SQL script itself. Make sure that you copy any changed migrations back to source control. 85 86 - Re-deploy the migration: 87 88 ```npm 89 npx prisma migrate deploy 90 ``` 91 92 ### Option 2: Manually complete migration and resolve as applied 93 94 The following example demonstrates how to manually complete the steps of a migration and mark that migration as applied. 95 96 - Manually complete the migration steps on the production database. Make sure that any manual steps exactly match the steps in the migration file, and copy any changes back to source control. 97 98 - Resolve the migration as applied - this tells Prisma Migrate to consider the migration successfully applied: 99 100 ```npm 101 npx prisma migrate resolve --applied "20201127134938_my_migration" 102 ``` 103 104 ## Fixing failed migrations with `migrate diff` and `db execute` 105 106 :::info 107 **Prisma v7 note**: The `--url` flag has been removed from `prisma db execute`. To run these commands against a production database, you'll need to configure the production database URL in your `prisma.config.ts` file before running `db execute`. You can create a separate config file for production (e.g., `prisma.config.prod.ts`) and use `--config prisma.config.prod.ts` to specify it. 108 ::: 109 110 To help with fixing a failed migration, Prisma ORM provides the following commands for creating and executing a migration file: 111 112 - [`prisma migrate diff`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-cli-reference#migrate-diff) which diffs two database schema sources to create a migration taking one to the state of the second. You can output either a summary of the difference or a sql script. The script can be output into a file via `> file_name.sql` or be piped to the `db execute --stdin` command. 113 - [`prisma db execute`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-cli-reference#db-execute) which applies a SQL script to the database without interacting with the Prisma migrations table. 114 115 This section gives an example scenario of a failed migration, and explains how to use `migrate diff` and `db execute` to fix it. 116 117 ### Example of a failed migration 118 119 Imagine that you have the following `User` model in your schema, in both your local development environment and your production environment: 120 121 ```prisma title="schema.prisma" showLineNumbers 122 model User { 123 id Int @id 124 name String 125 } 126 ``` 127 128 At this point, your schemas are in sync, but the data in the two environments is different. 129 130 You then decide to make changes to your data model, adding another `Post` model and making the `name` field on `User` unique: 131 132 ```prisma title="schema.prisma" showLineNumbers 133 model User { 134 id Int @id 135 name String @unique 136 email String? 137 } 138 139 model Post { 140 id Int @id 141 title String 142 } 143 ``` 144 145 You create a migration called 'Unique' with the command `npx prisma migrate dev -n Unique` which is saved in your local migrations history. Applying the migration succeeds in your dev environment and now it is time to release to production. 146 147 Unfortunately this migration can only be partially executed. Creating the `Post` model and adding the `email` column succeeds, but making the `name` field unique fails with the following error: 148 149 ```bash 150 ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'paul' for key 'User_name_key' 151 ``` 152 153 This is because there is non-unique data in your production database (e.g. two users with the same name). 154 155 You now need to recover manually from the partially executed migration. Until you recover from the failed state, further migrations using `prisma migrate deploy` are impossible. 156 157 At this point there are two options, depending on what you decide to do with the non-unique data: 158 159 - You realize that non-unique data is valid and you cannot move forward with your current development work. You want to roll back the complete migration. To do this, see [Moving backwards and reverting all changes](#moving-backwards-and-reverting-all-changes) 160 - The existence of non-unique data in your database is unintentional and you want to fix that. After fixing, you want to go ahead with the rest of the migration. To do this, see [Moving forwards and applying missing changes](#moving-forwards-and-applying-missing-changes) 161 162 #### Moving backwards and reverting all changes 163 164 In this case, you need to create a migration that takes your production database to the state of your data model before the last migration. 165 166 - First you need your migration history at the time before the failed migration. You can either get this from your git history, or locally delete the folder of the last failed migration in your migration history. 167 - You now want to take your production environment from its current failed state back to the state specified in your local migrations history: 168 - Run the following `prisma migrate diff` command: 169 170 ```bash wrap 171 # Prisma 6 172 npx prisma migrate diff \ 173 --from-url "$DATABASE_URL_PROD" \ 174 --to-migrations ./prisma/migrations \ 175 --shadow-database-url $SHADOW_DATABASE_URL \ 176 --script > backward.sql 177 178 # Prisma v7 (with production config) 179 npx prisma migrate diff \ 180 --from-config-datasource \ 181 --to-migrations ./prisma/migrations \ 182 --config prisma.config.prod.ts \ 183 --script > backward.sql 184 ``` 185 186 This will create a SQL script file containing all changes necessary to take your production environment from its current failed state to the target state defined by your migrations history. 187 188 - Run the following `prisma db execute` command: 189 190 ```bash 191 # Prisma 6 192 npx prisma db execute --url "$DATABASE_URL_PROD" --file backward.sql 193 194 # Prisma v7 (with production config) 195 npx prisma db execute --config prisma.config.prod.ts --file backward.sql 196 ``` 197 198 This applies the changes in the SQL script against the target database without interacting with the migrations table. 199 200 - Run the following `prisma migrate resolve` command: 201 202 ```npm 203 npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back Unique 204 ``` 205 206 This will mark the failed migration called 'Unique' in the migrations table on your production environment as rolled back. 207 208 Your local migration history now yields the same result as the state your production database is in. You can now modify the datamodel again to create a migration that suits your new understanding of the feature you're working on (with non-unique names). 209 210 #### Moving forwards and applying missing changes 211 212 In this case, you need to fix the non-unique data and then go ahead with the rest of the migration as planned: 213 214 - The error message from trying to deploy the migration to production already told you there was duplicate data in the column `name`. You need to either alter or delete the offending rows. 215 - Continue applying the rest of the failed migration to get to the data model defined in your `schema.prisma` file 216 - Run the following `prisma migrate diff` command 217 218 ```npm 219 npx prisma migrate diff --from-config-datasource --to-schema schema.prisma --config prisma.config.prod.ts --script > forward.sql 220 ``` 221 222 This will create a SQL script file containing all changes necessary to take your production environment from its current failed state to the target state defined in your `schema.prisma` file. 223 224 - Run the following `prisma db execute` command: 225 226 ```npm 227 npx prisma db execute --config prisma.config.prod.ts --file forward.sql 228 ``` 229 230 This applies the changes in the SQL script against the target database without interacting with the migrations table. 231 232 - Run the following `prisma migrate resolve` command: 233 234 ```npm 235 npx prisma migrate resolve --applied Unique 236 ``` 237 238 This will mark the failed migration called 'Unique' in the migrations table on your production environment as applied. 239 240 Your local migration history now yields the same result as the state your production environment is in. You can now continue using the already known `migrate dev` /`migrate deploy` workflow. 241 242 243 ## Prisma Migrate and PgBouncer 244 245 You might see the following error if you attempt to run Prisma Migrate commands in an environment that uses PgBouncer for connection pooling: 246 247 ```bash 248 Error: undefined: Database error 249 Error querying the database: db error: ERROR: prepared statement "s0" already exists 250 ``` 251 252 See [Prisma Migrate and PgBouncer workaround](/orm/v7/prisma-client/setup-and-configuration/databases-connections/pgbouncer) for further information and a workaround. Follow [GitHub issue #6485](https://github.com/prisma/prisma/issues/6485) for updates. 253

Yes — this is a documented, supported pattern, not a hack.

**Recommended approach: expand-and-contract data migration**, per `apps/docs/content/docs/guides/database/data-migration.mdx`:
1. Add the migration via `prisma migrate dev` as normal (schema change only).
2. Write a separate TypeScript script using Prisma Client to run the DML (e.g., `UPDATE`-style logic via `tx.post.update()` in a `$transaction`) — placed alongside the migration folder, e.g. `prisma/migrations/<timestamp>/data-migration.ts`, and run it manually against prod (not auto-applied by `migrate deploy`).

**Alternative: raw SQL in a generated migration file**, per `.../prisma-migrate/workflows/customizing-migrations.mdx` — you generate an empty migration with `prisma migrate dev --create-only`, then hand-edit `migration.sql` to add your DML statements before applying. This is the officially supported way to add custom SQL (including data-only statements) to migration history, not "hacky."

Prisma does **not** auto-generate DML like your lowercase-email example — you must author it yourself via one of the two methods above.
